You should not be unusually tired with the lifestyle you describe, certainly not at that age.

See a doctor. There are a variety of conditions which might explain your fatigue, anything from a hormone imbalance to a sleep disorder to an anemia or an unnoticed infection. A simple physical exam, some routine blood tests, and perhaps a sleep study will likely be all you need.

If that doesn't fix your problem come join us at /v/cfs and we can discuss the next step...
Coffee coffee coffee... if you don't enjoy it, learn to.
Isn't coffee just a temporary boost that results in needing to rest and sleep more later?

I start my day off with coffee (too much by most people's standards I'm sure) but it gets me through a 15 hour day at work and then I come home and crash. I find it helpful to stimulate my brain in to awake mode and then it lasts me the rest of the day. You may also just be overloaded and stressed out... try cutting one thing out of your day and see how that goes. Maybe when you find a place you will be less exhausted.

Things I guess I'd consider:

  • Do you use caffeine? If you do it irregularly, that could cause tiredness, as you'd intermittently go into caffeine withdrawals. Use it regularly or not at all. Also consider any other habit-forming chemicals you may consume. This actually does include excessive amounts of sugar, high-fructose corn syrup particularly, as some have mentioned.

  • Have you been told you snore, particularly that you stop breathing at night? That could be apnea, which would disrupt your sleep and can be dangerous as you get older.

  • General bloodwork might reveal something, definitely go see a doctor.

  • Are you allergic to anything? I have a few severe environmental allergies (particular plants that grow in the wild), and if I get near them, it makes me feel all sorts of sick, tired, etc.

  • You mention studying a lot, but do you have time for at least a little bit of a social life? Is your mood, aside from tiredness, generally okay? You've said it's gotten worse over the weeks, which makes me think it may be something you've adopted as you incorporated school into your routine. People do need to socialize, and you are in college - don't be afraid to take a night off every now and again and be with some friends, if you aren't. Not saying you need to go get shitfaced, just go forget about studying for a couple hours.

My social life consists of meeting other students to study with them. I've also considered that too little mental-resting time might be holding me back. Feels kind of counterintuitive though, "study less so you can study more".

It's a bit too early to go see a doctor, but I'll definitively go ahead if this holds up.

In Sweden I would be concerned about vitamin D deficiency. It is formed in the skin by exposure to sunlight when the sun is high in the sky. It is easy to get no sunlight during higher education, especially at high latitudes and during the darker parts of the year. The treatment is skin exposure when the sun is highest in the sky, or supplement pills. In the U.S. supplement pills are widely available. I take 1400 IU a day of vitamin D pills. I spent years waiting for death before I figured out I need extra vitamin D.

Another factor is mental collapse. Call it burnout, call it depression, call it whatever. Intense activity over your personal threshold can bring it on. Look up the treatments for depression on the web. Depression isn't a rare monster, and specific thinking habits and behaviors can help a lot.
